sweep_summary: Only one title-keyword item exists for tila1239: Turnbull 2017 (JIPA 47(3):251-282, doi:10.1017/S0025100316000384), already listed and already held; It is about the Acazulco variety, not Tilapa proper: one lexically placed prominent ('tonic') syllable per word, prefixes pre-tonic, tonic syllables longer/louder/higher; Turnbull calls it a possible 'pitch accent' system and explicitly does not extend it to Tilapa. It refines rather than contradicts the catalog's MORPHOLOGICAL coding (stem prominence with affixal/proclitic material outside), while showing that within-stem position is lexical in Acazulco citation nouns. The best direct stress statement read in this sweep is Hernández-Green 2015 (CIESAS dissertation, open, on file since 9/16): first syllable of native words is the prominent, longest syllable, foot ˈσσ, TAM proclitics unaccented — confirming the coding and recommended as co-primary for the languoid, but it does not supersede Palancar 2012, which remains the only statement on Tilapa proper. new_statements.quote: La mayoría de las palabras nativas tienen una estructura monosilábica o bisilábica como en (10a) y (10b). En estas palabras, el tono léxico está asociado con la primera (o única) sílaba, que es la sílaba prominente. ... En el caso del otomí de Acazulco, el peso de la sílaba está relacionado directamente con su duración: la sílaba más larga corresponde a la sílaba prominente. La sílaba prominente en monosílabos es, evidentemente, la única sílaba, mientras que en bisílabos es la primera sílaba. ... podemos decir que el pie métrico básico de la lengua es ˈσσ.
new_statements.translation: Most native words are monosyllabic or disyllabic as in (10a) and (10b). In these words the lexical tone is associated with the first (or only) syllable, which is the prominent syllable. ... In Acazulco Otomi, syllable weight is directly related to duration: the longest syllable is the prominent syllable. The prominent syllable in monosyllables is obviously the only syllable, while in disyllables it is the first syllable. ... we can say that the basic metrical foot of the language is ˈσσ. (fn. 13: in a Praat sample of 133 disyllables the second syllable averages 61.4% of the first syllable's duration.)

new_statements.locator: Sec. 1.1.2 'Prosodia', printed pp. 26-27 (pdf pp. 37-38), incl. fn. 13-14; also Sec. 1.2 ex. (32) printed p. 43 (nouns and adjectives each keep first-syllable accent) and Sec. 3.3 printed pp. 173-174 (TAM markers 'carecen de acento primario', analysed as proclitics)
new_statements.reading: First-hand, instrumentally supported statement that word prominence in the Acazulco variety is fixed on the first syllable of the (native) word/stem, that lexical tone anchors there, that each member of an adjective+noun sequence keeps its own first-syllable accent while true compounds take one primary accent on the first element, and that the preverbal TAM markers lack primary accent and are proclitics. That is stem-initial prominence with the proclitic cluster outside, the same configuration the catalog codes MORPHOLOGICAL from Palancar 2012's parenthetical on inflected verbs; it extends the rule to nouns. It sits in tension with Turnbull 2017 (same variety), whose citation-form nouns show a lexically placed tonic syllable (second syllable in roughly 38% of disyllables); Turnbull's finding concerns tone anchoring in isolation forms rather than a stress rule, and he does not claim a competing stress placement.

(2) Deciding source is a 2012 morphology article whose stress statement is one parenthetical limited to inflected verbs; thin on its own, but it is the only description of Tilapa proper, and the languoid's best phonological sources are Turnbull 2017 (held) and Hernández-Green 2015 (fetched sources now from the CIESAS open repository). (3) Hernández-Green 2015 pp.24-27, 43, 173-174 independently states for the Acazulco variety that the prominent (longest) syllable is the first syllable of native words (basic foot 'σσ, Praat duration measure on 133 disyllables), lexical tone anchors on it, nouns and adjectives each keep first-syllable accent, and TAM markers lack primary accent and are proclitics -- i.e. stem-in

sources.citation: Turnbull, Rory. 2017. The phonetics and phonology of lexical prosody in San Jerónimo Acazulco Otomi. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 47(3): 251-282 (online 2016-10-18). doi:10.1017/S0025100316000384. [Glottolog id 553681, hhtype phonology; already_listed]
sources.quote: p. 261: "2. Each lexical word has one and only one tone, which is lexically associated with one and only one syllable (the 'tonic' syllable)." fn. 10: "the syllable associated with the pitch peak of the first rise in the word is the tonic syllable. If there is no pitch rise (as in the falling or flat contours), then the tonic syllable is the first one." p. 273: "SJAO is argued to feature one prosodically prominent syllable per word (as per Leon & Swadesh 1949); nevertheless, these tonic syllables contrast in underlying tone (as per Sinclair & Pike 1948). ... This current analysis could be termed a 'pitch accent' system, as opposed to a 'tonal' system."
sources.locator: Sec. 2.2.2, p. 261 (axioms 1-2 and fn. 10) and p. 262 (axioms 3-4, Tables 6-7); Table 4, p. 259 (contour counts by word length); pp. 264-265 (prefixes are pre-tonic, get default L); Sec. 3, p. 273 (phonetic correlates); Sec. 4, p. 273 (discussion)
sources.note: Instrumental study (584 tokens of 266 words, mostly bare monomorphemic nouns in isolation, one elderly male speaker; p. 258) of the Acazulco variety, not Tilapa proper. Claims one prosodically prominent ('tonic') syllable per word whose position is lexical, not fixed: in disyllables the tonic is initial in the flat+falling contours (9.7%+50.3%) and second in the rising+rising-falling contours (25.0%+12.9%) (Table 4, p. 259); loans vs native and mono- vs multimorphemic words showed no difference (p. 259).
